newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraq allows U.N. to take missile parts abroad.
newsitem.headline: Iraq allows U.N. to take missile parts abroad.

text.p: Iraq has agreed to let the United Nations take scrapped missile engines out of the country for examination, U.N. arms envoy Rolf Ekeus said on Sunday.

"The government of Iraq agreed to the removal of remnants of proscribed missile engines from Iraq for in-depth analysis by the commission," Ekeus, chairman of the U.N. Special Commmission on Iraq (UNSCOM), told reporters in a joint news conference with Iraqi Foreign Ministry Undersecretary Riyad al-Qeisi.
The United Nations wants to establish if scrapped parts are from missing Soviet-made engines as Iraq maintains or are local equipment buried to divert attention from hidden missile engines.
Ekeus arrived in Baghdad on Thursday and held extensive meetings with Deputy Prime Minister Tareq Aziz during a four-day visit that ended with a joint statement outlining future cooperation.

Ekeus did not say when the approximately 100 scrapped engines and parts packed in boxes at U.N. headquarters in Baghdad would be removed. He said he intended to take them to laboratories in either the United States or France.
Earlier Iraq had objected to shipping parts to the United States, although it said it would allow inspection in Russia or France.
The components were unearthed in excavations last year. Iraq said it destroyed the missiles in 1992 and Ekeus said unilateral scrapping of banned items by Iraq had complicated his work.
He said Iraq claimed to have unilaterally dismantled a large portion of its long-range missiles and production tools. "This you can imagine creates a lot of deep concern," he said.

Ekeus did not say how many missiles he believed were missing but said Iraq could still be concealing equipment. Under terms of the ceasefire that ended the 1991 Gulf War that drove Iraq from Kuwait, Baghdad cannot have missiles with ranges greater than 150 km (93 miles).
"It does not mean that we reached any conclusion," Ekeus said of the missile deal.

Qeisi denied Iraq was hiding any banned material: "There is no policy of concealment on the part of the government of Iraq. We and UNSCOM are well on the way...to see to it that various files of proscribed weapons are closed."

Ekeus said his commission still had "quite substantial and serious" concerns about Iraq's chemical arms, which are also banned. He said the two sides agreed to put off discussion of Iraq's banned biological warfare programme until his next visit in March.
Ekeus must certify Iraq has no weapons of mass destruction before the United Nations will lift curbs on Iraqi oil exports, although Baghdad is allowed limited oil exports under a humanitarian deal.
